chapter: Lucky Roberts, Armstrong and the big-band rivalries
title: Rex Stewart takes on Armstrong at the Lenox and Rhythm Club
summary: Butler recounts Armstrong's visits to Harlem, Rex Stewart's triumph on Slew Foot Stomp at the Lenox Club, rival trumpeters at the Rhythm Club, and Armstrong's effect at the Lafayette.

story.theme_name: Working with and around Louis Armstrong
story.community_name: Playing with and around Louis Armstrong

blocks.x: You also heard him like in person in the twenties and thirties?
Well, I heard him when I was at the Lenox Club. Because, you see, he was working downtown in the pit, I think it was Lee Leslie's Black Birds. And Ray Smith was with Fletcher Henderson.

Rex Stewart, yeah. Well, see, Rex Stewart -- yeah, Rex Stewart was playing a lot of horn. He was playing a lot of horn. He was playing another thing and he was partners. So what happened, Louis Armstrong had went back to Chicago and come up to the Savoy Ballroom for about three nights. So Metcalf was up there, he had a band, he had a crown on his head. And Metcalf, he knew Louis Armstrong so he took the crown off. "He was my buddy."

So then, the first set, we took it off and that was good. And the second night, Rex took off from his job, because guys would take off to come and get you. He took off from his job and he come up to the Savoy Ballroom and got just as many hands as Louis got. Everybody said, man, Rex got it. Rex was all right, yeah.

So everybody on Sunday night, they'd go to -- they'd have that midnight thing. Everybody's going to the Lenox Club. Had (inaudible) Louis Armstrong, King on the trumpet (inaudible) because he's been working all day, they played just ordinary, you know. Sounded beautiful. Rex Stewart got up there and said, "I'm going to play one." And got up there and broke the house up. Beautiful. I mean broke it up.

He's got a funny way of laughing. "Now, I think I'll play another one." And he played a thing called "Slew Foot Stomp." And when he got through that third chorus, and people was standing up on the tables, and Rex grabbed a man's derby and tore it up, the man come out with something, a razor, wanted to get in -- "Here's your $10.00." They calmed the man.

And that was it. That was it. That was it, man. And that was the end of everybody challenging Louis Armstrong after that. But they had a lot of people doing these things. One time in the Rhythm Club, they heard him in there and I think it was -- Rex couldn't get there then, a boy named Sidney DeParis says, "I'm the greatest trumpet," everybody's saying, "I'm the greatest trumpet in America." And then they got down to the greatest trumpet in New York. Then they got down to the greatest trumpet in Harlem. 132nd Street, I'm the greatest trumpet in here.

And somebody sneaked a horn in Louis Armstrong's band. You had to use certain sandwiches and thing, you know. Potato salad -- you know, had this steam table. Louis started working. Cats jumped up on the table; feet on the food; stomping---that was the end of that.
That was the kind of stuff like -- the Lafayette Theatre:

I seen him in, he's making them 100 C's and when they got finished they had to (inaudible) and tear up all them lights and get that fire department effect. That's what that was. If he was there, he could create that kind of thing. So when they put them 100 C's and everybody's clapping, and the people clapping with him. Pandemonium set in. That's one man, just one man. When he yells, my goodness. So that was it. So that's what it was.
